analysis.one_liner: Repeals the FCC's 2003 media ownership deregulation and restores the old ownership limits.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 100 cosponsors, never received a committee vote and died at the end of the 108th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: In June 2003 the FCC loosened the rules that limit how many TV and radio stations and newspapers one company can own in a market and nationwide. This bill would have canceled those new FCC rules outright and put the stricter, older limits back in place, retroactively, and stopped the FCC from automatically reviewing and loosening those rules again. It would have kept a few large companies from buying up more local TV and radio outlets.
analysis.who_benefits: Viewers and listeners, especially in smaller markets, who would be more likely to get locally produced news, multiple independent voices, and varied programming. Local news staffs and community groups that rely on diverse outlets also benefit. Owners of the remaining independent stations gain because fewer large groups can buy them out.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Viewers and listeners in local markets

how_it_helps.text: The bill voids the FCC rules announced June 2, 2003, which relaxed limits on broadcast media ownership [S2].
It reinstates, retroactively to June 2, 2003, every ownership rule in effect on June 1, 2003, as if the FCC proceeding never happened [S3].
It bars the FCC from using its biennial review authority to further loosen broadcast ownership rules, removing a scheduled pathway for future deregulation [S2, S3].
The bill was sponsored by Rep. Bernard Sanders, an independent, and drew 100 cosponsors — 97 Democrats and 3 Republicans [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Large broadcast and media conglomerates, which lose the ability to own more stations in the same market, combine with newspapers, and expand their national reach. They also bear the cost of unwinding deals structured under the looser rules, since the old limits apply retroactively.

drawbacks.text: Rolling back rules retroactively could disrupt transactions and investments that companies made in reliance on the June 2003 rules; the bill applies the old limits retroactively to June 2, 2003 [S3].

Defenders of the FCC's update argued the old caps were written for a pre-internet, pre-cable media world, and that rigid statutory-style limits could prevent consolidation-driven investment in stations; the bill instead locks in the pre-2003 caps by statute [S2, S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit to ordinary people is preserving ownership diversity in local news and talk radio, which research and public comment at the time tied to local coverage and viewpoint variety. The main cost falls on media companies, which would face stricter limits and possible unwinding of deals. The retroactive feature is legally awkward and could be disruptive, but the core tradeoff is straightforward: fewer very large media owners versus more freedom for the largest owners to grow.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, moved to its Telecommunications subcommittee, and never got a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bernard Sanders introduced the bill on June 12, 2003, responding to the FCC's June 2, 2003 loosening of broadcast media ownership rules [S1, S2].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S5].
Twelve days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications and the Internet, where it stayed [S5].
The bill attracted 100 cosponsors — 97 Democrats and 3 Republicans — but no committee action or vote followed before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S4, S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest broadcast and media companies were better off: the FCC's looser ownership rules stayed in effect while the bill sat without a vote, and the committee with jurisdiction never took it up.

for.name: Rep. Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to invalidate the FCC's 2003 media ownership deregulation and restore the prior limits.

for.name: 100 House cosponsors (97 D, 3 R)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it broad if mostly Democratic support.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over telecom and FCC bills
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill; it was referred to a subcommittee on June 24, 2003 and stayed there.

against.name: FCC majority (Chairman Michael Powell)
against.what_they_did: Adopted the June 2, 2003 rules loosening media ownership limits that the bill sought to overturn; the agency majority favored the deregulation and Congress's telecom leadership did not reverse it.

against.name: Large broadcast and media companies
against.role: Networks and station groups (e.g., Clear Channel, Fox, Tribune, Viacom)
against.what_they_did: Lobbied for and publicly favored the ownership deregulation that the bill would have rolled back.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was an independent and the cosponsor list was overwhelmingly Democratic (97 of 100), with only 3 Republicans; the committee that buried it was controlled by Republicans.

industries.industry: Large broadcast and TV station groups
industries.note: The FCC's 2003 rules raised limits on how many TV stations one company could own nationwide and eased cross-ownership of newspapers and broadcasters [S2, S3]. The bill cancels those gains, so the biggest station groups lose the chance to buy more outlets. Their interest in the deregulation ran against viewers' interest in diverse local owners.

Radio ownership caps were a central part of the FCC's ownership proceeding, and the bill restores the prior, stricter limits [S3]. Consolidation in radio had reduced local programming variety, so a reversal favors listeners.
The loosened rules would have allowed more combinations of newspapers with broadcast stations in the same market; the bill reinstates the ban, keeping papers and TV stations separately owned.
Stricter ownership caps make it harder for large groups to buy up independent stations, preserving locally owned outlets and the local jobs and coverage that come with them.
